title: HKMA Circular B1/15C & A.R.T. Framework: Technical Compliance Guide (Principles 1–9)
subtitle: Deconstructing HKMA Circular B1/15C across Principles 1–9 (Accountability, Resiliency, Trust): operationalising 3LoD model risk governance, automated drift telemetry, and sovereign in-VPC containment before sandbox graduation.
summary: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) Circular B1/15C and the collaborative HKMA-Cyberport Generative AI Sandbox define the definitive supervisory baseline for Authorised Institutions (AIs) deploying generative models in banking. This technical guide decomposes the 9 High-Level Principles across Accountability (Principles 1–3), Resiliency (Principles 4–6), and Trust (Principles 7–9), establishing the engineering, model validation, and governance gates required for sandbox graduation.

sections.title: Executive Supervisory Context: Circular B1/15C & The GenAI Sandbox Graduation Gate
sections.content:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), in strategic partnership with Cyberport, launched the Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Sandbox alongside supervisory Circular B1/15C titled "Supervisory Guidance for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence". This landmark supervisory instrument moves beyond general statements of principle, establishing binding technical and governance requirements for Authorised Institutions (AIs) deploying generative models across front, middle, and back-office banking operations.

While initial exploration within the HKMA GenAI Sandbox allows regulated entities to pilot use cases—ranging from risk analysis copilots to bilingual customer interaction summarizers—graduation from the sandbox into live production requires verifiable compliance with the A.R.T. (Accountability, Resiliency, Trust) supervisory framework.

Under Circular B1/15C, supervisory scrutiny focuses not merely on model capability, but on containment architecture: Authorised Institutions must mathematically demonstrate model stability, continuous telemetry, and local execution boundaries before live customer or ledger data may interact with generative reasoning pipelines.

sections.title: Accountability (Principles 1–3): Three Lines of Defence (3LoD) & Board Governance
sections.content:
Principles 1 through 3 of Circular B1/15C mandate explicit allocation of senior management responsibility and robust Model Risk Management (MRM) operationalisation:

* Principle 1 (Board & Senior Management Oversight): Ultimate accountability for AI outcomes remains non-delegable. Boards and designated Executive Committees must approve AI risk appetites, oversee systemic deployment risks, and ensure dedicated resource allocation. A nominated Senior Executive must hold formal accountability for each live model family.
* Principle 2 (Three Lines of Defence Operational Demarcation):
  - 1LoD (Business Units & ML Engineering): Directly responsible for model training, prompt engineering, daily output reviews, and incident reporting.
  - 2LoD (Model Risk Management & Compliance): Conducts independent validation, bias evaluation, adversarial stress testing, and maintains the comprehensive Model Inventory.
  - 3LoD (Internal Audit): Independently audits the adequacy and effectiveness of the MRM framework and model execution logs.
* Principle 3 (Documentation & Provenance Integrity): Every production model must maintain an immutable provenance trail—recording foundational model weights, system prompts, fine-tuning datasets, and human evaluation scores.

sections.title: Resiliency (Principles 4–6): Continuous Drift Telemetry, Cybersecurity & In-VPC Containment
sections.content:
Principles 4 through 6 govern operational resilience, cyber defense, and runtime containment under HKMA SPM TM-E-1:

* Principle 4 (Continuous Telemetry & Concept Drift Monitoring): Generative models cannot be evaluated solely at pre-deployment. Financial desks must implement automated telemetry monitoring for semantic drift, retrieval index degradation, token entropy anomalies, and hallucination rates. When concept drift exceeds pre-agreed tolerance thresholds (e.g. Wasserstein distance > 0.05), automated circuit breakers must suspend autonomous outputs.
* Principle 5 (Cybersecurity & Adversarial Confinement): Protection against OWASP LLM Top 10 vulnerabilities, including direct/indirect prompt injection, model inversion attacks, and supply chain contamination. All tool execution (via MCP or function calling) must operate in sandboxed, privilege-limited runtime containers.
* Principle 6 (Business Continuity & Fail-Safe Fallback): Authorised Institutions must demonstrate deterministic fallback mechanisms. If external inference endpoints degrade or fail, business operations must immediately revert to rule-based or human-operated manual workflows without operational disruption.

sections.title: Trust (Principles 7–9): Data Privacy, Synthetic Disclosures & Customer Recourse
sections.content:
The Trust dimension enforces ethical, legal, and transparency guardrails:

* Principle 7 (Personal Data Protection & PDPO Alignment): In accordance with Hong Kong Cap. 486 (PDPO) and PCPD AI guidelines, no customer personal data may be utilized for foundation model pre-training or external vendor fine-tuning without explicit, informed consent. Real-time inference pipelines must incorporate sub-millisecond PII tokenisation and masking.
* Principle 8 (Synthetic Content Transparency): Clear visual and textual labeling of all AI-generated advice, communications, and documentation. Customers must be explicitly informed when they interact with conversational generative agents.
* Principle 9 (Explainability & Customer Recourse Channels): Where AI models impact credit underwriting, loan limits, or account security, institutions must provide explainable logic and establish accessible human escalation channels for customer recourse and manual dispute adjudication.

sections.title: Technical Architecture: Zero-Cloud-Egress In-VPC Deployment Model
sections.content:
To satisfy HKMA inspection teams, tier-1 institutions must bypass commercial multi-tenant public APIs. The approved sovereign deployment architecture mandates:

1. Private In-VPC Containerization: Weights hosted on dedicated customer hardware or private VPC instances with zero public internet routing.
2. Deterministic Regulatory Compiler: Replacing probabilistic prompts with deterministic policy gates (such as PEARL) that compile regulatory rules into executable validation binaries in <10ms.
3. Cryptographic Proof of Non-Retention: Mutual verification verifying zero retention of prompt or inference artifacts on third-party cloud infrastructure.
4. Local Boundary Proof: Mathematical Negative Proof ensuring foreign regulations (such as EU AI Act high-risk classification) are excluded, preventing multi-million dollar scope bloat.

summary: SFC Circulars 24EC55 and 26EC32 establish strict regulatory boundaries for Licensed Corporations (LCs) deploying Generative AI and autonomous agentic workflows in Type 1, 4, and 9 regulated activities. This whitepaper provides a comprehensive engineering and compliance blueprint covering Manager-in-Charge (MIC) accountability regimes, deterministic citation pinning, material non-public information (MNPI) DLP firewalls, and red-teaming against indirect prompt injection.

sections.title: Regulatory Demarcation: SFC Circulars 24EC55 & 26EC32 for Licensed Corporations
sections.content:
The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has established a robust supervisory perimeter for Generative AI adoption through Circulars 24EC55 ("Use of Generative AI by Licensed Corporations") and 26EC32 ("Cyber Resilience and Adversarial Guardrails in Algorithmic and Agentic Workflows").

These circulars establish that Licensed Corporations (LCs)—specifically those holding Type 1 (Dealing in Securities), Type 4 (Advising on Securities), and Type 9 (Asset Management) licenses—retain absolute fiduciary and regulatory responsibility for the accuracy, fairness, and security of all AI-generated or AI-assisted research and advice.

Under the SFC regulatory framework, technological complexity cannot be invoked to excuse compliance failures. LCs deploying large language models, agentic workflows, or automated research copilots must institute formal controls matching the speed and risk profile of automated synthesis.

sections.title: The Manager-in-Charge (MIC) Regime: Non-Delegable Algorithmic Accountability
sections.content:
Under the SFC Manager-in-Charge (MIC) regime, algorithmic automation does not diminish executive culpability. Circular 24EC55 makes clear that designated MICs hold direct personal accountability:

1. MIC for Overall Management Oversight: Accountable for corporate-wide AI risk appetite, capital allocation, and supervisory reporting.
2. MIC for Risk Management: Accountable for independent 2LoD validation, continuous drift evaluation, and approving model risk thresholds.
3. MIC for Information Technology: Accountable for infrastructure containment, VPC air-gapping, secret management, and cyber resilience under 26EC32.
4. MIC for Compliance: Accountable for verifying that automated outputs adhere strictly to the SFC Code of Conduct (including General Principles 1–3 on honesty, fairness, and diligence).

Designated MICs must execute formal sign-offs on AI deployment charters. Relying on vendor assurances or unverified cloud SaaS terms of service is explicitly deemed a supervisory violation.

sections.title: MNPI Containment & Data Loss Prevention (DLP) Boundaries
sections.content:
A central concern of SFC Circular 24EC55 is the accidental leakage or cross-contamination of Material Non-Public Information (MNPI). When research analysts or portfolio managers query an LLM regarding sensitive M&A transactions, earnings embargoes, or block trading interests, any data egress to public cloud providers creates catastrophic regulatory exposure under Part XIII / XIV of the Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO, Cap. 571) regarding insider dealing.

Mandatory MNPI safeguards include:
* Complete Data Egress Isolation: LLM inference engines must operate within dedicated, private VPC boundaries where egress traffic to public endpoints is blocked at the routing layer.
* Zero Retention Agreements: Where managed enterprise foundation models are accessed, cryptographic and contractual guarantees must prove zero training, zero logging, and zero persistent prompt caching.
* Information Barrier (Chinese Wall) Enforcement: Vector stores and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) indexes must strictly mirror internal Chinese Walls. An equity research copilot must never index private wealth management records or investment banking transaction workspaces.

sections.title: Deterministic Citation Pinning & Hallucination Elimination Protocol
sections.content:
Under Circular 24EC55, investment advice or research distributed to institutional or retail clients cannot rely on unverified generative text. To satisfy the SFC's standard of reasonable basis and due diligence (Code of Conduct Paragraph 3.4):

1. The Citation Pinning Protocol: Every statistical figure, price target, earnings forecast, or statutory reference generated by an AI research assistant must be pinned to an immutable primary source chunk (e.g. audited annual reports, HKEX regulatory filings, or statutory circulars).
2. Automated Grounding Scoring: Unpinned factual claims must be automatically detected and quarantined by an evaluation layer prior to human review.
3. Mandatory Human-in-the-Loop (HITL): Research reports and investment recommendations distributed to clients must bear the signature and verified sign-off of a licensed Responsible Officer (RO) or licensed representative who verifies the pinned citations.

sections.title: Adversarial Robustness & Cyber Containment (Circular 26EC32)
sections.content:
Circular 26EC32 addresses the emerging threat landscape of agentic AI systems, focusing on cyber resilience against automated adversaries:

* Indirect Prompt Injection: Malicious third parties embedding hidden prompt overrides in public financial disclosures, analyst PDF memos, or market data feeds. LCs must implement dual-model token verification and context-boundary sandboxing.
* Model Context Protocol (MCP) Firewalls: When agentic copilots are granted tool-calling capabilities (e.g. database querying or API invocation), all tools must be strictly read-only and governed by an immutable MCP schema registry. Arbitrary shell execution or outbound HTTP requests must be physically blocked.
* Adversarial Red-Teaming: LCs must conduct recurring adversarial penetration testing before deploying agentic capabilities into production, verifying that jailbreak attempts cannot bypass MNPI filters or compliance boundaries.

subtitle: Mathematical negative proof boundary analysis under SFC Code of Conduct Schedule 7: proving why internal LLM investment research copilots fall outside algorithmic order routing and DMA requirements, eliminating Day-1 scope creep.
summary: SFC Code of Conduct Schedule 7 imposes rigorous pre-trade testing, kill switches, and market access controls on algorithmic trading and Direct Market Access (DMA) systems. When asset managers deploy internal LLM research copilots, compliance teams frequently suffer from severe scope creep, erroneously applying Schedule 7 algorithmic trading mandates. This paper establishes the formal mathematical negative proof demonstrating why internal research copilots are legally and architecturally exempt.

sections.title: The Compliance Scope Dilemma: The Algorithmic Trading Misconception
sections.content:
When licensed asset managers (SFC Type 9) and advisory firms (SFC Type 4) deploy artificial intelligence to synthesize research, summarize corporate filings, or calculate DCF valuations, internal compliance committees frequently experience severe scope paralysis. External legal advisors and risk officers frequently confound 'algorithmic trading' with 'algorithmic reasoning', threatening to subject internal research copilots to the onerous requirements of Schedule 7 to the SFC Code of Conduct.

Schedule 7 mandates exhaustive pre-trade risk controls, automated kill switches, ultra-low-latency real-time market risk monitors, and annual direct market access certifications. Applying these requirements to an internal research summarizer creates immense compliance friction—delaying deployment by 6 to 9 months and adding hundreds of thousands of dollars in unnecessary consulting fees.

The solution requires establishing an airtight, mathematically provable demarcation boundary between internal decision support systems and regulated algorithmic trading facilities.

sections.title: Statutory Analysis of SFC Code of Conduct Schedule 7 & DMA Requirements
sections.content:
Under paragraph 1.1 of Schedule 7, 'Algorithmic Trading' is defined strictly as:
'computer trading where each order is generated automatically based on a predefined mathematical model or algorithm, without human intervention in determining any of the trading parameters (including price, volume, timing, or whether to submit the order)'.

Key statutory criteria establishing the statutory boundary:
1. Automated Order Generation: Systems that directly formulate and route trading orders to exchange matching engines or alternative liquidity pools (ALPs).
2. Elimination of Human Discretion: Execution occurring without an intervening human trader exercising independent judgment over order submission.
3. Market Impact Potential: Systems capable of injecting sudden liquidity shocks, runaway feedback loops, or erroneous order floods into live market venues.

In contrast, an internal research copilot operates exclusively in the pre-ideation knowledge synthesis plane. It analyzes financial filings, drafts investment memos, and answers analyst queries. It possesses zero network connectivity to the Order Management System (OMS) or Execution Management System (EMS).

sections.title: The Mathematical Negative Proof Architecture: Formal Demarcation
sections.content:
To provide absolute assurance to internal audit and the SFC, licensed entities must not rely on verbal assurances. They must compile a formal mathematical Negative Proof.

Formally, let S be the state space of the AI copilot system, and O be the set of valid order creation actions in the firm's trading infrastructure.
The Negative Proof establishes:
∀ s ∈ S, P(ExecutionAction(s) ∈ O) = 0

This is enforced through four immutable architectural gates:
1. Physical Network Disconnection: The inference VPC has no peering, route, or gateway leading to the FIX protocol trade execution network.
2. Read-Only Data Plane: Database connectors used for ingestion are restricted to read-only replica credentials with DROP/INSERT/UPDATE permissions revoked at the database engine level.
3. API Contract Schema Enforcement: The copilot's output schema is constrained strictly to textual markdown and structured analytical JSON—incapable of packaging FIX order payloads.
4. Cryptographic Assertion Hash: Every compiled software release generates a signed attestation hash verifying the absence of trading execution libraries.

summary: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD) published the Model Personal Data Protection Framework for Artificial Intelligence under the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (PDPO, Cap. 486). sections.title: The Day-2 Compliance Drift Trap: How Financial AI Silently Breaches PDPO
sections.content:
A systemic vulnerability across Hong Kong financial institutions is the divergence between initial AI deployment approvals and subsequent operational realities—a phenomenon termed 'Day-2 Compliance Drift'.

On Day 1, an enterprise AI research copilot is approved by the Data Protection Officer (DPO) and Legal Counsel based on a pristine, synthetic dataset containing only public HKEX disclosures and anonymized market commentary.
On Day 2, internal engineering squads seeking to enhance utility connect the copilot to internal client CRM repositories (e.g. Salesforce), communication archives (e.g. Bloomberg chat, client emails), or wealth onboarding forms.

Instantly, the model begins ingesting Personal Identifiable Information (PII)—including client names, HKID numbers, net worth statements, and investment risk profiles. Without immediate supervisory intervention, the firm enters active, ongoing breach of the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (PDPO, Cap. 486), exposing executive leadership to criminal penalties, statutory enforcement notices, and devastating reputational damage.

sections.title: PCPD Model Personal Data Protection Framework: The 4 Core Pillars
sections.content:
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD) established the Model Personal Data Protection Framework for Artificial Intelligence to guide organisations in the ethical and compliant adoption of generative systems. The framework rests on four operational pillars:

1. AI Strategy & Governance: Formulating a comprehensive AI strategy, establishing an internal AI Governance Committee, and allocating senior executive accountability.
2. Risk Assessment & Human Oversight: Conducting comprehensive Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) proportional to the risk profile, and establishing clear levels of Human-in-the-Loop (HITL), Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL), or Human-out-of-the-Loop oversight.
3. Data Protection in AI Model Lifecycle: Enforcing data minimization across training, fine-tuning, and inference stages. Prohibiting the use of sensitive personal data for model re-training without explicit consent.
4. Stakeholder Communication & Transparency: Providing transparent Personal Information Collection Statements (PICS), disclosing AI usage, and maintaining accessible channels for data access and correction requests under Cap. 486.
sections.contentHtml:
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data (PCPD) established the Model Personal Data Protection Framework for Artificial Intelligence to guide organisations in the ethical and compliant adoption of generative systems. The framework rests on four operational pillars:

Pillar 1: Strategy & Governance

AI Governance Committee charter, executive allocation, and data classification policies.

Pillar 2: Risk Assessment & HITL

Mandatory Privacy Impact Assessments (PIA) and defined human oversight intervention levels.

Pillar 3: Lifecycle Data Protection

Strict data minimization, PII tokenisation, avoiding unvetted model re-training.

Pillar 4: Transparency & Recourse

Updated PICS declarations, AI disclosure labels, and statutory data subject rights fulfillment.

sections.title: Operationalising Data Protection Principles (DPPs 1–6) in LLM Architectures
sections.content:
Financial institutions must translate the six Data Protection Principles (DPPs) of Schedule 1 to the PDPO into technical runtime constraints:

* DPP 1 (Purpose & Manner of Collection): Personal data collection must be lawful, fair, and necessary. AI models must enforce input-side filtering to reject unneeded personal attributes.
* DPP 2 (Accuracy & Retention): Personal data must be accurate and up-to-date, and retained no longer than necessary. In RAG architectures, outdated customer profiles must be purged synchronously from vector indexes.
* DPP 3 (Use Limitation): Personal data collected for account servicing cannot be repurposed to train general investment models without fresh, explicit consent.
* DPP 4 (Data Security): Practical measures to protect personal data against unauthorized access or processing. Vector embeddings containing sensitive customer context must be encrypted at rest and in transit.
* DPP 5 (Openness & Transparency): Clear disclosure of policies and practices through updated PICS regarding AI data processing.
* DPP 6 (Data Subject Access & Correction): Establishing technical procedures to identify, retrieve, and correct or delete customer data embedded in vector retrieval databases.
sections.contentHtml:
Financial institutions must translate the six Data Protection Principles (DPPs) of Schedule 1 to the PDPO into technical runtime constraints:

  • DPP 1 (Purpose & Manner): Enforcing input-side filtering to reject unneeded personal attributes before LLM ingestion.
  • DPP 2 (Accuracy & Retention): Automated TTL (time-to-live) expiration and synchronization on vector retrieval indexes.
  • DPP 3 (Use Limitation): Cryptographic purpose limitation blocking cross-departmental data contamination.
  • DPP 4 (Data Security): Field-level encryption for vector embeddings and ephemeral prompt cache deletion.
  • DPP 5 & 6 (Openness & Access): Standardized PICS disclosure and deterministic mechanisms to excise data from retrieval indexes.

sections.title: Automated PII Tokenisation & High-Speed Redaction Engine
sections.content:
To enable financial desks to leverage generative intelligence without triggering PDPO violations, institutions must deploy an automated pre-inference tokenisation layer.

The Local Tokenisation Engine Architecture:
1. Sub-Millisecond Pattern & Entity Recognition: Detects Hong Kong Identity Card (HKID) numbers, bank account numbers, credit card numbers, passport identifiers, and client names in <2ms.
2. Reversible Vaulting: Replaces sensitive identifiers with synthetic surrogate tokens (e.g. [HKID_0x8F32] or [CLIENT_ID_4821]) before the prompt reaches the inference container.
3. Post-Inference Reconstruction: For authorized users within secure boundaries, the output text is re-hydrated with original identifiers, ensuring analysts see full context while the underlying model weights and log stores never touch raw PII.
4. Zero External Dependency: Built entirely with deterministic compiled logic—ensuring zero external API calls or latency spikes.

sections.title: Continuous Telemetry & Compliance Drift Circuit Breakers
sections.content:
Mitigating Day-2 drift requires active, real-time monitoring rather than point-in-time audits. Enterprise architectures must incorporate:

* Vector Store Ingestion Scanners: Daily telemetry scanning all vector embeddings for anomalous entropy or unexpected personal data ingestion.
* Prompt Drift Circuit Breakers: Real-time inspection analyzing prompt streams. If a user or automated agent attempts to submit un-redacted client records, the circuit breaker trips—quarantining the session and alerting the compliance officer.
* Automated Re-Certification: Every 30 days, or upon any change to data source connections, the policy engine re-evaluates the system architecture against PCPD standards to confirm zero compliance drift.

sections.title: Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) Matrix & PCPD Audit Checklist
sections.content:
To demonstrate proactive accountability under PCPD guidance, compliance teams must maintain a living Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) matrix:

1. Data Flow Mapping: Comprehensive diagram showing every data source, ingestion pipeline, tokenisation gate, and storage location.
2. Statutory Legal Basis Analysis: Explicit justification under DPP 1 and DPP 3 for all processed data elements.
3. Residual Risk Assessment: Quantitative risk scoring for data re-identification, model inversion attacks, and prompt injection leaks.
4. PCPD Audit Dossier: Pre-compiled documentation ready for regulatory submission in the event of an inquiry or complaint.
